e.t: This word is a proper name rendered as “Abaisan” or “Avesan.” It identifies a named figure in the Greek Old Testament, rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears twice, both times in Judges 12, at Judges 12:8 and Judges 12:10. Since no verse wording is provided here, the name itself can be explained confidently, while the person’s specific role must be understood from those passages.

Aboubos, also rendered Avuvos, is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Maccabees 16.11 and 16.15. The name itself does not carry an ordinary translated meaning in these records; its function is to identify the individual named Aboubos. Understanding what happens in either reference requires the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX adverb means “without fear.” It describes an action or manner carried out fearlessly, indicating that a person acts without being afraid. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 2:32. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the absence of fear in the way something is done.

Azōtios, also written Azotios, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. Its meaning is therefore the identification of the named person, place, or group in the passage, while the surrounding verse determines which one is intended. This name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented by the LXX, in two verses: Joshua 13:3 and 1 Samuel 5:3. The name itself does not provide further description apart from identifying what is named.

This noun refers to injurious treatment—behavior that harms, mistreats, or wrongs someone—and can also describe an affront, a deliberate insult or indignity. It names an injury done through hostile or insulting treatment rather than a physical object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in the Deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense is harmful treatment or an insulting offense.

This noun means “compulsion” or “necessity”: a condition in which someone is compelled or something must happen. It describes pressure or unavoidable need rather than a voluntary choice. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 38 times, so it can refer broadly to circumstances that leave little or no freedom to act otherwise. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This noun means “accursed”: something placed under a curse or regarded as under a curse. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes a condition or designation rather than an action. The word occurs 24 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, with many occurrences in Joshua and several in Deuteronomy. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its use there.

Ananias is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs 36 times, appearing across Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. Because it is a proper name, its meaning here is chiefly identification: it distinguishes a particular person named Ananias. The surrounding verse is needed to identify which Ananias is intended and what that person does in a given passage.

This adjective describes someone or something as bald on the forehead. It identifies hairlessness specifically at the front of the head, rather than serving as a general word for every kind of baldness. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 13:41. That single occurrence marks the word as a precise physical description; the surrounding verse is needed to explain its role there.

This adjective means “human” or “humanely,” describing what belongs to people or is done in a human way. In the Greek Old Testament and related Jewish writings, it occurs 14 times, including passages in Numbers, Job, Ezekiel, Daniel, and 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense distinguishes ordinary human beings or human manner from what is divine, heavenly, or otherwise beyond human life. The surrounding sentence determines whether it describes a person, something associated with people, or an action carried out with human consideration.

This adjective describes someone who shows no pity and acts without mercy—“pitiless; ruthless.” It portrays a hard, unfeeling attitude toward others rather than compassion or kindness. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:4. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a person or action marked by merciless severity.

Antiochis is a proper name identifying a person named Antiochis. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is primarily the person’s name rather than a concept to define. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:30. The precise significance of the person in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This Greek LXX verb means “carry away” or “carry off.” It describes taking something or someone from one place to another, with the emphasis on removal or transfer. The word appears 25 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it can describe various acts of carrying away rather than one special kind of removal. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being moved and the surrounding sentence.

Arem is a proper name, functioning as the personal designation of an individual in the Greek Old Testament text. It occurs once, in Nehemiah 12:15. The available lexical meaning is simply “Arem,” so the word identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. Its precise referent and role must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself is a personal name.

This noun refers to an original or an originator—the one connected with beginning something or standing at its source. It identifies a person in terms of being first or initiating, rather than merely participating afterward. In the Greek Old Testament and related books represented here, it occurs 29 times, so its basic sense is used across multiple passages while its precise reference depends on the surrounding context.

This adjective describes someone or something that has suffered no injury or damage: unhurt and unharmed. It presents the person or thing as remaining safe and whole despite circumstances that might have caused harm. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word appears only twice, both times in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains clear: being preserved from injury rather than wounded, damaged, or impaired.

Astarte is a proper name used for a named figure in the Greek Old Testament. The word itself identifies Astarte rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. It occurs five times in the LXX, in Joshua, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, and 2 Chronicles. Because the available word-level information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise significance in any one passage must be understood from that passage’s context.

Apher, also rendered Afer, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. The name occurs twice in the LXX corpus, appearing once in Genesis 25:4 and once in 1 Chronicles 4:17. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific family or historical setting must be understood from those passages.

Balek, also rendered Valek, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 5:8. The name itself does not carry an additional ordinary meaning in the available lexical definition; its function is to identify the individual named in that passage.

This noun refers to a “buzzing crowd”—a gathered multitude perceived through its combined, murmuring sound. It describes the crowd as a noisy collective rather than focusing on any one person. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs once, in Baruch 2:29. Its precise force in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is a crowd whose presence is marked by buzzing or humming noise.

This adjective means “eaten,” describing something that has been consumed as food. It identifies the condition or use of an object in relation to eating, rather than naming the act of eating itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Judges and once in Job. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains something eaten or fit in relation to being eaten.

This LXX Greek noun refers to a taste or the flavor of something. It describes what is sensed when food or another substance is tasted, and it can also point to the character or quality perceived from that taste. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, including passages in Exodus, Numbers, Job, Jeremiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its central idea remains the experience or quality of taste, while the surrounding sentence determines what substance or comparison is being discussed.

Geon or Yion is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings. It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears three times in this LXX corpus: once each in Genesis, Jeremiah, and Sirach. The available lexical information gives the name itself, but not enough surrounding verse text to explain its particular reference in each passage.

This noun refers to a medium or a familiar spirit—someone or something associated with seeking communication from the spirit world. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 23:24. The word’s basic sense identifies this kind of occult person or spirit rather than describing an ordinary messenger, counselor, or prophet. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its lexical meaning remains centered on a medium or familiar spirit.

This Greek LXX verb means “flow through.” It describes something moving as a liquid through or across a place. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 2 Maccabees 10:20. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the movement of liquid through something or along a course.

This Greek LXX noun refers to pursuit, especially the hostile pursuit of someone—persecution. It describes being chased, pressured, or hunted by opponents rather than simply making a peaceful journey. In the LXX, it occurs three times across Proverbs, Lamentations, and 2 Maccabees. The word can therefore name either the act of pursuing or the suffering brought upon those who are pursued. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

This Greek word means “present,” describing the act of giving something as a gift or bestowing it on someone. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming the gift itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Jewish Scriptures, it occurs five times, each in a different verse, including passages from Genesis, Leviticus, Esther, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its precise force in any one passage depends on what is being given and to whom, but the central idea is a gift freely bestowed.

Iroth is a proper name, referring to a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It is rendered as “Iroth” and appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Numbers 33. The available word information identifies the name but does not specify whether Iroth refers to a person or a location. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding passage and the name’s use there.

This LXX verb means “leap out”: it describes a movement that springs or jumps outward from a place. It presents action rather than a person, object, or quality, so its basic focus is on sudden outward motion. The word occurs six times in the LXX corpus, across four Old Testament occurrences and two deuterocanonical occurrences. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a leap or spring outward.

This word means “willing”: it describes someone who chooses or intends to do something freely rather than being forced. As an adjective, it identifies a person or action marked by readiness and consent. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Exodus and once in Job. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what the person is willing to do in each passage.

This verb means to persevere or continue—to keep going rather than stop. It describes sustained action or persistence, and its wording presents continuation as an ongoing activity. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs eight times, all in Sirach. The surrounding verse determines what a person continues in or persists through, but the word itself emphasizes remaining engaged over time. Its basic sense is steady continuation, whether the action is difficult, prolonged, or simply required to carry something forward.

Enemetiim is a proper name, referring to a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Genesis 10:13, and is rendered “Enemetiim.” The available wording identifies the name but does not provide a further definition or explain whether it designates a person, location, or group. Its exact reference therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun refers to sending someone or something away—an expulsion or removal from a place or situation. It names the act or result of being sent away rather than the person who performs it. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:4. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is being expelled and what role the term plays there, but its basic sense remains the forcible or deliberate sending away of someone or something.

This Greek LXX verb means “expound” or “explain”: to make something understandable by describing or interpreting it. It is an action word, referring to the act of giving an account or making meaning clear rather than merely mentioning something. The verb occurs eight times in the Greek LXX, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing a repeated use for communicating understanding. One English rendering is “explain,” which matches its central sense. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes someone or something as “bent over” or “crooked.” It points to a posture or shape that is not upright or straight, rather than naming an action. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:5. The word’s precise force there depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic sense remains a bent or crooked condition or appearance.

This Greek LXX verb means “allure” or “drag by”: it describes drawing or pulling someone or something along, whether by attraction or force. As a verb, it presents an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs ten times in the Greek LXX, across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and situation.

This verb means “howl at”—to cry out toward someone or something in a loud, distressed, or hostile way. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Zechariah 11:8. The word describes an action rather than a person or object, so its central idea is the act of making a howling cry directed at another. The surrounding verse is needed to determine the precise force of that cry in its setting.

Eregaba is a proper name, rendered as “Eregaba” or “Eregava.” It identifies a person or place named in the Greek Old Testament, rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. The name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Kings 4:13. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its particular referent must be established from that passage; the lexical sense itself is the name “Eregaba” or “Eregava.”

This Greek LXX noun refers to “stirring up; exciting”—the act or effect of provoking movement, agitation, or heightened feeling. It describes something that rouses or unsettles rather than remaining calm and inactive. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Deuteronomy and once in Sirach. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains the stirring or exciting of someone or something.

Esi is a personal name, identifying a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 2:52. Because the available information does not include the verse’s wording or surrounding passage, it is not possible to say more about Esi’s identity or role from the name alone. The name functions simply as a proper noun used to distinguish this individual from others in the genealogy.

Esrieli, also rendered Ezrili, is a proper name. It functions primarily to identify someone by name rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in Numbers 26:35. The available wording gives the name itself, but no further contextual description is provided here, so its precise reference in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage.

Euin, also given as Ein, is a proper name rather than a common word with a general definition. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Numbers 31:8, identifying a named figure in that passage. The name itself does not describe an action, quality, or object; its function is to designate someone by name. Understanding exactly who is meant and what role he has requires the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This Greek LXX noun means “good conduct”: behavior that is upright, proper, and worthy of approval. It describes the quality of acting well rather than merely possessing a good reputation. The word appears twice in the Greek text of 3 Maccabees, in 3 Maccabees 3:5 and 3:6. Its central idea is a pattern of honorable behavior, and the surrounding passage determines the particular aspect of that conduct being emphasized.

This word means “treasury,” referring to a place where valuable goods or funds are kept. It is a noun, so it names the storehouse itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 28:11. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is a designated place for storing wealth or valuable possessions.

Iedaia, also rendered Iethea, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 3:10. As a proper name, its main function is to identify a particular person in the biblical record. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain that person’s role or significance there; the name itself simply distinguishes the individual from others.

Iesi is a proper name, referring to a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:42. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide the verse’s surrounding text, it does not establish an additional meaning or description for Iesi. Its significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the people and events described in the surrounding context.

This noun refers to a kite, a particular bird identified in the Greek Old Testament. The term names the bird itself rather than an action, quality, or person. It appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Leviticus and once in Deuteronomy, with both occurrences rendered “kite.” Its precise role in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains the name of this bird.

Isoam is a proper name rendered as “Isoam.” It functions as a name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) material represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 24:27. Since the lexical information gives the name itself rather than a separate definition, its ordinary meaning is simply Isoam; the surrounding verse is needed to identify the person or role associated with it.

This word is a proper name for a person, rendered “Iōchabed” or “Iokhaveth.” It functions as a personal name rather than as a description, action, or general title. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Exodus and once in Numbers. The available wording identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse context would be needed to explain what is being said about the person in either passage.

Karchēdōn, also given as Karkhithon, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in Isaiah 23, appearing in verses 1, 6, 10, and 14. The name identifies the same named subject throughout those occurrences; its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means “deluge”: to overwhelm with a great flood or a mass of water. It describes an action rather than a person or thing. The word occurs nine times in the Greek LXX, across seven Old Testament occurrences and two Deuterocanonical occurrences. Its uses include passages in Job, Psalms, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Wisdom, showing that it can describe flooding in varied scriptural settings. The precise force in any particular verse depends on that verse’s surrounding context.

This verb means “hide away”—to put something or someone out of sight or keep them concealed. It describes an action rather than a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 15 times, mostly in the Old Testament books, and its use commonly concerns concealment or removal from view. The surrounding verse determines whether the hiding is temporary, protective, secretive, or related to an object being put away. Its central idea remains the deliberate act of hiding something away.

This Greek LXX adjective means “left behind,” describing someone or something remaining after others have gone, been taken, or been set apart. It can identify what remains in a group or situation rather than naming an action itself. The word occurs 97 times across 89 Old Testament verses in the Greek LXX, so its basic sense is used broadly for people or things that remain. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This noun means “contempt” or “disdain”: a settled attitude of looking down on someone or treating them as unworthy of respect. It describes scorn rather than simple disagreement or dislike. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains an attitude of disrespect or contempt toward another person or matter.

This noun refers to “one that butts”—a creature or being that thrusts against something with its head or horns. It identifies the one doing the butting rather than describing the action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both in Exodus 21, where the references concern an ox known for this behavior. The word therefore points to a habitual or recognized tendency to butt, especially when describing an animal whose conduct creates danger for people or other animals.

This word is a proper name referring to “Kēdar” or “Kithar.” It identifies a named person or people in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs 12 times in 11 Old Testament verses, from Genesis through Song of Songs, including passages in Genesis, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function remains that of a name.

This Greek LXX verb refers to “fleece” or “wool,” describing a concrete material rather than a person, place, or abstract quality. As a verb, it expresses an action involving fleece or wool. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Deuteronomy 18:4. Its basic meaning is therefore limited and straightforward: fleece or wool. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding Greek wording and context.

This Greek LXX adverb means “secretly,” describing an action done without being openly seen or known. It tells how something happens rather than naming a person, object, or event. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Jeremiah, so its basic sense is clear but its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. It expresses concealment or lack of public openness, without by itself explaining the motive behind the hidden action.

This adjective means “preventive”: it describes something intended to stop, hinder, or keep an unwanted result from happening. It focuses on action taken beforehand rather than repair afterward. The word appears three times in the Greek LXX corpus, all in 4 Maccabees, so its recorded use is limited but consistent with this basic sense. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on what is being prevented and the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “employed” or “minister,” describing someone engaged in assigned service or work. It is used for active service rather than merely holding a title. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 99 times, showing a broad use for people carrying out duties in worship, community life, or other appointed responsibilities. The exact force in a particular passage depends on its surrounding context, but the central idea remains purposeful service or employment.

This noun refers to “snuffers; bowls”—objects used among the temple furnishings or vessels. It names practical equipment rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, in Jeremiah 52:19, within a list of items taken from the temple. The precise function of these objects in that passage is understood from their place among the other vessels, but the word itself points to snuffers and bowls as distinct physical objects.

Meētabēl, also rendered Mitavil, is a proper name referring to a person rather than a general word or action. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Nehemiah 6:10. The name itself identifies an individual, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain that person’s role in the event. This entry preserves the name as a personal designation, not as a translated concept with a broader definition.

Melchisa is a proper name referring to a person. The name appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in 1 Samuel: 1 Samuel 14:49 and 1 Samuel 31:2. Its recorded meaning is “Melchisa,” also rendered “Melkhisa,” so it functions as a personal name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name itself does not provide further meaning without additional contextual information from the surrounding verses.

This verb means “withdraw; move on,” describing a person or thing leaving one place and proceeding elsewhere. It expresses movement away or onward rather than remaining where one is. In the Greek Old Testament writings represented here, it occurs five times, in Wisdom and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or who is moving and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains departure or continued movement.

This Greek LXX verb means to eat food regarded as unclean. It describes the act of consuming such food, rather than naming the food itself or expressing a general word for eating. The word occurs nine times in the Greek LXX corpus, all in 4 Maccabees, across eight verses. Its meaning is stated plainly as “eat unclean food,” so the central idea is the violation or observance of a food restriction expressed through eating. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Nabaiōth, also rendered Naveoth, is a proper name used as a personal or place designation in the Greek Old Testament. The name appears five times in the LXX, across Genesis, 1 Chronicles, and Isaiah. Because it is a proper name rather than a descriptive word, its meaning is primarily the identity it names, not an idea or action. Its exact reference in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Noe is a proper name referring to the biblical person known in English as Noah. It functions as a personal name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, Noe occurs 50 times, appearing especially in Genesis and also in several later books. The name is found in passages from Genesis 5 through 7 and in later references, preserving the same personal designation throughout this Greek corpus.

This Greek LXX noun means “pain,” referring to physical or inward suffering. It describes distress that can be experienced as an ongoing burden or sharp affliction. The word appears 62 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, with especially frequent use in Job, Isaiah, and Psalms. Its ordinary meaning remains focused on the experience of pain rather than on a particular cause or outcome. The surrounding verse determines whether the pain is bodily, emotional, or connected with distressing circumstances.

Onias is a proper name used for a person named Onias. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs 23 times across 22 verses, chiefly in 2 Maccabees, and also in 1 Maccabees, 4 Maccabees, and Sirach. The word itself identifies a name rather than describing an action, quality, or general category. Its particular significance in any passage must come from that passage’s surrounding text.

This noun refers to passion or temperament—the strong emotional disposition or feeling a person has. It can describe an inward force that shapes a person’s responses and conduct. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs 280 times, showing that it is used broadly across biblical writings rather than being limited to one situation. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains a person’s passionate or temperamental disposition.

This word is a proper name, referring to a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It is rendered as “Oulaimaradach” or “Ulemarathakh,” preserving the name rather than translating it as an ordinary descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 52:31. Since no verse text or surrounding context is available here, the person’s role and the significance of the name in that passage cannot be explained from this word alone.

This verb means “make water,” referring plainly to the act of urinating. It is a physical action word rather than a title, name, or description of a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in four verses, so it is uncommon within this corpus. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the bodily act of making water.

This noun refers to something put alongside another thing—an appendage or attached addition. It describes an item considered in relation to something else, rather than standing as the main object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Exodus, where its basic sense concerns an accompanying or added part. The surrounding verse determines exactly what object is being described, but the word itself points to something placed beside or joined to another thing.

This verb means “bend.” It describes the action of making something curve or move away from a straight position. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 15:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central lexical idea remains the action of bending. The word functions as an action word rather than a name or description of a person.

e.h: A Bearer of a Light Shield
e.t: This noun means “one who bears a light shield,” describing a lightly equipped shield-bearer or soldier. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in 2 Chronicles. The word identifies a person by the kind of defensive equipment he carries, rather than naming a weapon or a military action. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a soldier equipped with a light shield.

This verb means “stay around for” or “wait for,” describing someone who remains present while expecting or awaiting a person or thing. It focuses on continued waiting rather than a brief pause. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Genesis and once in Wisdom. Its precise emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

This word means “pine,” referring to the evergreen tree. It is a noun used for the name of a kind of tree rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs once, in Isaiah 60:13. The word’s precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its lexical meaning is simply pine.

This Greek Old Testament verb means to give someone a drink or to water something. It describes providing water for people, animals, or land, depending on the sentence. The word occurs 64 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Old Testament writings, so it covers both ordinary acts of supplying water and the watering of fields or plants. Its precise application in any particular verse depends on what receives the water and the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “set on fire”: it describes causing something to burn or placing it where fire can ignite it. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Ezekiel 24:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of setting something on fire.

This Greek LXX noun means “face” and can also describe what is “ahead of” someone or something. Its central idea is the front or visible presence of a person or thing. Depending on the sentence, it may refer to the face itself or to position before, in front of, or facing another. This word occurs 1,154 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its exact sense is determined by how the surrounding sentence uses the idea of a face or what lies before it.

This Greek LXX verb means “beat with rods” or “beat out,” describing forceful striking with a rod or similar implement. It is an action word rather than a general term for harm, and its exact force is determined by the surrounding sentence. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Judges and once in Ruth, so its established meaning is clear but its recorded use is limited. [1] [2]

This word is the proper name “Sabat,” also given as “Savat.” It functions as a name rather than as a general description or action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears twice: once in Zechariah and once in 1 Maccabees. The available wording consistently renders it as “Sabat,” while the lexical definition also preserves “Savat” as an alternative form. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse context.

Salisa is a proper name, functioning as the personal name of an individual in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a descriptive word with a broader meaning or concept. Salisa occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 7:37. Without the surrounding verse text, the name alone does not establish further details about the person or the significance of the reference.
